html:
Nazi Germany was the German state from 1933 to 1945, when Adolf Hitler and his Nazi Party ruled it as a dictatorship. They called it the Third Reich, and it started the Second World War.

Hitler became chancellor in January 1933, in the depths of the Depression. Within months his government banned other parties and unions, jailed opponents in the first concentration camps and took over the press. The Nazis taught that Germans were a superior race and that Jews were their enemy. They twisted old texts, such as Tacitus's Germania, into proof of a pure German past. Jews were pushed out of jobs and public life by the Nuremberg Laws of 1935, and many fled, such as the family of Anne Frank and scientists like Lise Meitner, who explained nuclear fission from exile in Sweden in 1938.

Germany rearmed, took Austria and Czech lands in 1938 and 1939, and invaded Poland in September 1939, which began the war in Europe. In occupied lands, and above all in the east, it killed on a vast scale: some six million Jews were murdered in the Holocaust, along with Roma, disabled people, Soviet prisoners and millions of Slav civilians. When the Red Army won back occupied lands, Stalin punished whole peoples he accused of helping the Germans, such as the Crimean Tatars.

Hitler killed himself in Berlin in April 1945, and Germany surrendered on 8 May. Its leaders were tried at Nuremberg. See Germany and the World Wars.
sum: Nazi Germany was the German state from 1933 to 1945, when Adolf Hitler and his Nazi Party ruled it as a dictatorship. They called it the Third Reich, and it started the Second World War.
